newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK press blames all sides for activist's death.
newsitem.headline: HK press blames all sides for activist's death.

text.p: Hong Kong newspapers on Friday pointed fingers of blame in all directions for the death at sea of an activist protesting Japan's claims of sovereignty to a disputed group of islands.

Protest leader David Chan was killed on Thursday when he jumped off a ship in the storm-whipped East China Sea to press China's claim to the islands, known in Japanese as the Senkakus and in China and Taiwan as the Diaoyus.
Fifty protesters gathered outside Japan's consulate here shouting "down with Japanese militarism".
They handed over petitions to consular staff urging Japan to quit the islands where Japanese rightwingers have built a lighthosue and raised the Japanese flag.

The words "shock" and "tragedy" screamed from headlines of the major Chinese and English language newspapers which blamed all governments embroiled in the territorial quarrel, Taipei, Beijing and Tokyo, as well as those involved in the protest.
Experts were also quoted as saying the tragedy could whip up a frenzy of anti-Japanese sentiment in this British colony which reverts to Chinese rule next year.

"The recovery of the Diaoyu Islands, now under Japanese occupation, is a cause worth dying for," the English-language Hong Kong Standard said in its editorial. "It was a brave gesture, if not a properly thought out one."
But it also ran results of a street poll which showed many members of the public disagreed with that view.

"Naturally people are extremely upset...there will be a lot of pressure because sentiments of Chinese people around the region reached extremes and this tragedy could well channel them towards destructive actions," China watcher Li Pang-kwong of Lingnan college was quoted by the Standard as saying.

"What makes the outcome doubly tragic is that it was all so unnecessary," said the South China Morning Post. "The whole escalating dispute over the Diaoyu Islands has been allowed to get progressively out of hand."
It said Japan could have eased tensions by removing symbols of Japan's sovereignty from the islands but "Tokyo failed to make that gesture and now a man is dead".
The Chinese-language Sing Pao said Tokyo, Beijing and Taipei should all shoulder responsibility for the tragedy.
If Japanese warships had not surrounded the freighter, and the Chinese and Taiwan governments had been willing to provide protection, the incident might have been avoided.
The Hong Kong Economic Times said the Chinese and Taiwan governments had been too weak to stand up to Japan.
"How many more Chinese have to die before the Chinese government will take concrete action?"
The mass-circulation Oriental Daily put the blame on Japan. It said if Tokyo had not laid claim to the Diaoyu Islands, Chan would not have organised the protest trip and been killed.

The Beijing-funded daily Wen Wei Po defended China's restrained position on the dispute, saying that Beijing was doing its best to sort out the problem with Japan through diplomatic channels. It also praised Chan for his patriotism.
The China-controlled Ta Kung Pao said the determination of the Chinese people to protect the Diaoyus would not be undermined.
But it urged those carrying on the fight to keep cool heads and consider the big picture in working for the good of Hong Kong and the motherland.
